title: Tropical Storm Moke Threatens Hawaii With Flooding One Week After Lala
excerpt: The second tropical system in two weeks could dump up to 15 inches of rain on Hawaii's Big Island, where thousands remain without power from Hurricane Lala.
body:
• Tropical Storm Moke is forecast to pass south of Hawaii this weekend, bringing 5 to 15 inches of rain to the Big Island
  • More than 9,000 homes and businesses on the Big Island remain without power from Hurricane Lala, which struck last weekend
  • Flood watches are in effect for the Big Island from late Saturday through Monday afternoon
  • Airlines are preparing for a second round of flight disruptions as gusty winds and heavy rain approach

Tropical Storm Moke is advancing toward Hawaii, threatening the islands with another round of heavy rainfall and flash flooding just one week after Hurricane Lala caused widespread damage across the Big Island.

The National Hurricane Center said Saturday that Moke was located about 450 miles southeast of Hilo, Hawaii, moving west-northwest at 9 mph with maximum sustained winds of 45 mph. Forecasters expect wind speeds could reach up to 60 mph as the system strengthens during its approach.

A Battered Big Island Braces Again

The timing could hardly be worse. Hurricane Lala dumped up to 40 inches of rain on parts of the Big Island last weekend, triggering devastating floods and leaving more than 9,000 homes and businesses without power as of Saturday. Hawaiian Electric said most customers should have had power restored by August 21, but some areas in Ka'u may not see full restoration until September 8.

The National Weather Service has issued a Flood Watch for the Big Island from late Saturday night through Monday afternoon. Because the ground remains saturated from Lala, it may take less rainfall than usual to cause dangerous flash flooding.

"This rainfall may produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides for the windward and southeast Big Island, especially in steep terrain and over areas that were affected recently by Lala."

— National Hurricane Center advisory

Forecast Track and Expected Impacts

Moke is expected to pass farther south of Hawaii than Lala did — roughly 150 to 200 miles south of the Big Island, compared to Lala's 30-mile pass. While the wider berth offers some relief, the storm's moisture field extends well beyond its center.

The Big Island faces the heaviest rainfall: 5 to 10 inches are forecast, with isolated totals as high as 15 inches, according to the hurricane center. Rainfall will begin impacting the Big Island Saturday night into early Sunday before spreading to other islands through early next week.

Eastern Maui could see 1 to 4 inches, while the remaining islands face 1 to 2 inches. Gusty winds are expected across the island chain, particularly at higher elevations, with life-threatening swells and rip currents possible along east- and south-facing shores.

Airlines and Travelers Brace for Disruption

U.S. airlines serving Hawaii are monitoring the situation and preparing for potential cancellations, coming just days after Hurricane Lala forced widespread flight cancellations amid a state of emergency. The FAA issued a statement saying it is coordinating with carriers and air traffic control facilities in Hawaii.

The Hawaii Tourism Authority urged visitors traveling to or within the islands this weekend to monitor official forecasts and check directly with airlines, hotels, and activity providers for updates.

A Rare Two-Storm Stretch

Two tropical systems threatening Hawaii in two weeks is unusual and underscores the active Central Pacific hurricane season. Forecasters have noted that a weakening of El Niño's traditional hurricane shield — which tends to suppress storm formation near Hawaii — has contributed to the heightened activity this season.

Residents across the state are urged to make preparations before Moke's outer bands arrive and to avoid flood-prone roads and low-lying areas once rainfall begins.
